config.title: Module system

intro.title: Module system
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Node.js application that uses the module system to organize code into separate files. You will learn how to export functions and variables from one file and import them into another using `module.exports` and `require`. This introduces the core programming concept of modularity, which helps keep code clean, reusable, and maintainable. The main technologies involved are Node.js's built-in CommonJS module system and JavaScript files. By the end, you'll understand how to structure a basic project with multiple modules.
intro.usecase: The Node.js module system is fundamental to building scalable applications like e-commerce platforms, where product catalog, shopping cart, and payment processing are separate modules. In content management systems, modules organize user authentication, article editing, and media upload functionality. Developers use modules to create reusable components in web servers, API endpoints, and database connectors, enabling clean separation of concerns. This pattern appears in tools like Express.js routers, where each route file is a module handling specific endpoints.

objectives: Implement a custom module that exports functions and variables
Apply the require() function to import built-in Node.js modules
Construct a module that exports a default function using module.exports
Configure a module to export multiple named values using an object
Integrate multiple custom modules into a single main application file
Manipulate imported module data within your application logic
Initialize a project structure that separates code into logical modules

steps.title: Import the built-in Node.js fs module
steps.instruction: Use require() to import the built-in Node.js fs (file system) module and assign it to a constant variable named fs.
steps.hint: Use the require() function with the module name 'fs' and assign the result to a const variable.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing another built-in module
const path = require('path');
steps.expectedOutcome: The fs module is imported and ready to use for file system operations.
successCriteria: The fs module is imported using require() and assigned to a constant variable named fs.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using require('fs') and assigning it to a const variable named fs.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fs module needs to be imported. Use require('fs') and assign it to a constant variable.

steps.title: Create a module that exports a simple function
steps.instruction: Create a new file named 'greet.js' in the same directory. Inside this file, create a function named 'greet' that takes a 'name' parameter and returns a greeting string like 'Hello, [name]!'.
steps.hint: You'll need to create a separate file. The function should return a string that includes the name parameter. Use module.exports to make the function available to other files.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new file 'greet.js' is created with a function that returns a greeting and is exported using module.exports.
successCriteria: The greet.js file exists and contains a function named 'greet' that returns a greeting string and is exported with module.exports.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've created a separate file named 'greet.js' with a function that returns a greeting and exports it with module.exports.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a new file named 'greet.js', write a function named 'greet' that returns a greeting, and export it using module.exports.

steps.title: export this function using module.exports
steps.hint: You'll need to create a separate file. The function should return a string that includes the name parameter. Use module.exports to make the function available to other files.
steps.feedbackPartial: Review the instruction and try again.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction and try again.

steps.title: Import your custom module
steps.instruction: Use require() with a relative path to import the module you created in step 2. The module was exported from a file named 'myModule.js'.
steps.hint: Use require('./myModule.js') to import the module from the same directory.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing a local module
const myModule = require('./myModule.js');
steps.expectedOutcome: The custom module from step 2 is imported using require() with a relative path.
successCriteria: The custom module is imported using require('./myModule.js') or similar relative path syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the correct relative path to 'myModule.js'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import isn't quite right. Use require() with './myModule.js' to import the module from the same directory.

steps.title: Call the imported function
steps.instruction: Call the function you imported from your custom module and log the result to the console.
steps.hint: Use the function name you imported in step 3, followed by parentheses and a semicolon. Then use console.log() to display the returned value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The imported function is called and its return value is displayed in the console.
successCriteria: The function from your custom module is called and its result is logged using console.log().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're both calling the function and logging its return value.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're calling the function correctly and logging the result with console.log().

steps.title: Create a module that exports multiple values
steps.instruction: Create a new file named 'multipleExports.js' and define two functions inside it: 'add' that takes two numbers and returns their sum, and 'multiply' that takes two numbers and returns their product. Export both functions as named exports.
steps.hint: You can use either function declarations or arrow functions. Remember to use 'module.exports' with an object containing both functions.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new module file 'multipleExports.js' is created with two functions and exports them as an object.
successCriteria: The 'multipleExports.js' file exists, contains both 'add' and 'multiply' functions, and exports them using 'module.exports' with an object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure both functions are defined and exported correctly. Check that 'module.exports' contains both function names.
steps.feedbackWrong: The module wasn't created as expected. Ensure you create a new file, define both functions, and export them as an object.

steps.title: Import and use the multiple exports
steps.instruction: Import the module with multiple exports using destructuring to access its individual values.
steps.hint: Use destructuring syntax in the import statement to extract specific values from the module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Destructuring import example
const { value1, value2 } = require('./myModule');
steps.expectedOutcome: The module with multiple exports is imported using destructuring syntax.
successCriteria: The import statement uses destructuring to extract values from the module with multiple exports.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to use destructuring syntax in your import statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. Try using destructuring to import the individual values from the module.

steps.title: Use the fs module to read a file
steps.instruction: Use the fs.readFileSync() method to read the contents of a file named 'example.txt' and store it in a variable called fileContent.
steps.hint: Call fs.readFileSync('example.txt', 'utf8') to read the file synchronously with UTF-8 encoding.
steps.analogousExample:
// Reading a file synchronously
const data = fs.readFileSync('data.txt', 'utf8');
steps.expectedOutcome: The file 'example.txt' is read and its contents are stored in the fileContent variable.
successCriteria: The fs.readFileSync() method is called with 'example.txt' and 'utf8' arguments, and the result is assigned to a variable named fileContent.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using readFileSync() with the correct arguments and storing the result in a variable named fileContent.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try using fs.readFileSync('example.txt', 'utf8') to read the file and store the result in a variable.

steps.title: Handle file reading errors
steps.instruction: Wrap the existing fs.readFileSync() call in a try-catch block to handle potential errors.
steps.hint: Place the file reading code inside a try block, and add a catch block to log any errors that occur.
steps.expectedOutcome: The file reading operation is now protected with error handling, preventing crashes if the file doesn't exist or can't be read.
successCriteria: error is logged or handled appropriately
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have both a try block with the file reading code and a catch block that handles the error.
steps.feedbackWrong: The code doesn't show proper error handling. Remember to wrap the file reading in a try-catch block to handle potential errors.

steps.title: Create a module that exports a class
steps.instruction: Create a new file named 'Person.js' that defines and exports a class named Person with a constructor that takes name and age parameters and assigns them to instance properties.
steps.hint: Use the class syntax to define Person, then export it using module.exports.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new Person.js file is created with a class definition that is properly exported.
successCriteria: Person.js contains a class Person with a constructor that sets this.name and this.age, and exports it with module.exports.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the class has a constructor that sets instance properties and is exported correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you created a new file named Person.js with a class definition and export statement.

steps.title: Import and instantiate the class
steps.instruction: Import the class module you created earlier and create an instance of the class.
steps.hint: Use require() to import the module, then use the new keyword with the class name to create an instance.
steps.expectedOutcome: The class module is imported and an instance of the class is created.
successCriteria: The class module is imported using require() and an instance is created with the new keyword.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using require() to import the module and the new keyword to create the instance.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're importing the class module correctly and creating an instance with the new keyword.
